summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe, even semi-permanent colour service: consult and choose a shade that the client's natural level can actually show, do the skin and strand tests, protect the client, apply, time and rinse the colour, and give aftercare. You will also learn the basics of colour theory, how porosity changes the result, how to care for natural and relaxed hair, and how to handle, store and throw away colour products safely.

blocks.p: Semi-permanent colour is the gentle end of hair colouring. It adds tone, richness and shine, blends a little grey and refreshes faded colour, without lightening the hair and without a hard line of regrowth. For many clients it is the first colour they try, so a careful service builds trust for every colour service that follows. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees.

Gentle does not mean harmless. Semi-permanent colour can still stain skin and clothes, cause an allergic reaction, and come out patchy or darker than planned on porous hair. The unit is about **choosing the right shade, testing, protecting and timing** as much as brushing colour on.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon: a shade test board on different hair swatches, and a colour service on a model or practice head. The assessor watches your tests, protection, timing, evenness, safety and clean-up as well as the finished colour.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hair, the swatches and the record card. Never photograph a model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Feature
Temporary
Semi-permanent
Permanent (oxidative)
rows: Where the colour sits
On the outside of the cuticle only.
In and just under the cuticle; a little reaches the outer cortex.
Inside the cortex, where small colour molecules join into large ones that cannot wash out.
How it is made
Ready to use: rinse, spray, mousse, chalk.
Ready to use, or mixed with a mild, low-strength developer or activator for some deposit-only products.
Mixed with a developer (hydrogen peroxide), usually with ammonia or a substitute.
Can it lighten?
No.
No. It deposits colour only.
Yes, as well as adding colour.
How long it lasts
Until the next shampoo.
Fades over a number of shampoos, often 4 to 8 on healthy hair (follow the maker); fades faster on porous hair.
Until the hair grows out or is cut; the roots need a retouch.
Regrowth line
None.
None: it fades evenly, so grey and new growth blend in.
A visible line as the hair grows.
Skin test
Not usually.
When the maker says; allergy is still possible.
Always, as the maker says.

blocks.p: Semi-permanent colour is a **deposit-only** colour: it can put colour on the hair but cannot take natural pigment out. Its colour molecules are small, so they slip into the outer part of the hair, and small molecules wash out again a little each time the hair is shampooed. That is why the colour fades gradually and does not leave a regrowth line.

ul: Add richness, tone and shine to natural or already coloured hair.
Make the hair **the same level or darker**, never lighter.
Soften and blend grey: it tints grey hair, though grey hair may take the colour less deeply or faster-fading, and 100 per cent grey is not fully covered.
Refresh faded colour on the mid-lengths and ends of permanently coloured hair.
Cancel an unwanted tone (brassy gold or orange) by using the opposite tone.
Give a first-time client a low-commitment change, because it fades away.
Lighten hair, or make dark hair look blonde.
Show a bright or pale shade on dark hair: a bright red on very dark hair gives only a slight tint, seen mostly in strong light.
Cover white or very resistant grey fully.
Last as long as permanent colour.

blocks.note: Most semi-permanent colours contain no ammonia and are mixed with no developer, so they are usually kinder to natural and relaxed hair. Read the label anyway. Some 'demi-permanent' products use a low-volume developer and are a different service; do not mix them up with true semi-permanent colour.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Colour theory and choosing the shade

blocks.p: Hair colour is described by **level** (how light or dark) and **tone** (the colour you see). Levels run from 1 (black) to 10 (the lightest blonde) on the usual scale. Makers' charts show level and tone together, for example '4 – medium brown' or '5.4 – light copper brown'.

head: Level
Name
Level
Name
rows: Black
Dark blonde
Very dark brown
Medium blonde
Dark brown
Light blonde
Medium brown
Very light blonde
Light brown
Lightest blonde

blocks.p: Most Jamaican clients have natural hair at level 1 to 3. On those levels, semi-permanent colour gives a **tint** and added shine, not a visible change of shade. To see a clear colour the shade must be at the client's level or darker, or the hair must already have been lightened by another service.

head: Group
Colours
What to remember
rows: Primary
Red, yellow, blue
Cannot be made by mixing other colours.
Secondary
Orange (red + yellow), green (yellow + blue), violet (blue + red)
Each is made from two primaries.
Tertiary
Red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green, blue-green, blue-violet, red-violet
A primary mixed with its neighbouring secondary.
Complementary (opposites)
Red and green; blue and orange; yellow and violet
Opposites on the wheel cancel each other. This is how you neutralise an unwanted tone.

head: Unwanted tone in the hair
Cancel it with
Example
rows: Yellow, gold, brassy blonde
Violet (or ash with a violet base)
Violet toner on pale gold hair.
Orange, copper, brassy brown
Blue (an ash or cool tone)
Ash brown on orange-brown hair.
Red, red-brown
Green (a matt or natural tone)
A natural or matt shade to calm a red.
Green (from chlorine, for example)
Red
A warm tone over greenish hair.

ul: **Warm tones**: red, orange, copper, gold. **Cool tones**: blue, violet, ash, green.
**Natural** or neutral shades have a balance of both.
A tone on top of an existing tone mixes: a violet shade over yellow-gold hair neutralises it; a warm red over an orange base makes it hotter.
Underlying pigment matters. Dark hair has red and orange underneath, which is why brassy tones show when it is lightened or when the colour fades.

flow: Find the natural level in daylight, against the chart, on dry hair
Check how much grey there is and where
Note any existing colour, relaxer or lightening and the tone in the hair
Ask what the client wants, and show her the shade chart
Pick a shade at the same level or darker, with the tone you want
Tell her honestly what she will see, and how long it will last
Strand test, especially on the most porous part

head: Client's wish
Choice and honest advice
rows: 'A richer, shinier dark brown' on level 3 hair
A level 3 or darker shade in a warm or neutral tone. It will add depth and shine; it will not change the shade much.
'Bright burgundy' on level 2 hair
Only a slight red tint, seen mostly in strong light. If she wants it to show, she will need a service that lightens, which is a different unit.
'Get rid of the orange in my brown hair'
An ash or cool shade at her level; blue cancels orange. Expect a more natural, cooler brown.
'Cover the grey at my temples without a hard line'
A natural shade at her level; explain that grey may take it unevenly and the result is a softening, not full cover.
'Refresh the faded ends of my colour'
Apply to the faded mid-lengths and ends with a matching or slightly richer shade, as the maker allows.

blocks.note: Never promise a result you cannot deliver. 'It will add shine and a little depth, and it will fade over several washes' is honest. 'It will turn your hair burgundy' is not, on level 2 hair.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Ask or check
Why
rows: The result she wants, and a picture or shade chart
To agree what is possible before you begin.
Past colour, bleach, henna, home dyes, relaxers, perms and smoothing treatments, with dates
They change how the colour takes. Henna and metallic dyes can react with chemicals or block colour.
Past reactions to colour or any hair product; allergies
A past reaction means a skin test is essential, or no service with that product.
Medicines, pregnancy, illness
Hormonal changes and some medicines can make the scalp sensitive; follow the Centre's rules and the maker's instructions.
The scalp: cuts, sores, scratches, redness, flaking, infection
Colour on broken skin can sting, burn or cause an infection.
The hair: natural level, tone, grey, porosity, elasticity, condition, ends versus roots
To predict the result and prevent patchiness.

head: Finding
What to do
rows: Cuts, sores, weeping or inflamed areas on the scalp
Put off the service; suggest a doctor if it is sore or weeping.
Signs of an infection or infestation (lice, ringworm, impetigo)
No service. Refer kindly and privately; clean and disinfect.
A positive skin test (redness, itching, swelling)
Do not use that product. Record it.
A past severe reaction to colour
No service with that product.
Very weak, over-processed or damaged hair
Treat first; strand test; the maker may not allow colour.
Metallic salts or compound henna suspected
Do an incompatibility test; if it reacts, no colour service.

ul: Put a small amount of the colour, mixed as the maker says, on the skin behind the ear or inside the elbow. Let it dry and leave it uncovered.
Leave it for the time the maker says. **Often 48 hours** before the service, but follow the maker and the Centre.
A clear result means no redness, itching, swelling or blisters. Any reaction means no colour with that product.
Record the date, product and result. A clear test does not last for ever: repeat it as the maker says.

blocks.note: Even a gentle colour can cause allergy. If the maker asks for a skin test, it is not optional. Colour must never go on a client whose test was positive, who has not been tested when the maker requires it, or whose scalp is broken.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Apply the colour to a small, hidden section, time it as the maker says, rinse, dry and look at it in daylight.
It shows the **final shade**, whether porous parts take it darker, and whether the hair can take the colour without damage.
Do one on the most porous part (often the ends of long or relaxed hair), and another on the roots if the hair varies.

blocks.p: Skin tests protect the client's skin. Strand tests protect the hair and the result. They are separate tests and you may need both.

Porosity is how easily hair takes in water and products. A healthy cuticle lies flat, so healthy hair has low to normal porosity and takes colour slowly and evenly. Hair that is **porous** has a raised or damaged cuticle, so it soaks up colour fast. The ends of long hair are usually the most porous: they are the oldest part and have had the most sun, heat, combing and chemical services.

head: Hair
What happens with semi-permanent colour
What you do
rows: Healthy, low porosity
Colour enters slowly; may need the full time and gentle warmth if the maker allows.
Follow the maker's time; use a cap or gentle heat only if the maker says.
Porous ends, healthier roots
The ends take colour darker; the roots look lighter; patchy result.
Strand test; apply to the roots first and the ends later, or use a shorter time on the ends, as the maker allows.
Relaxed hair
Often porous, especially the lengths; may grab colour.
Strand test; leave the gap after a relaxer that the maker says.
Very damaged hair
Takes colour unevenly and loses it fast.
Condition and strengthen first; the maker may not allow colour.
Grey or white hair
May take colour less deeply or fade sooner; has a different texture.
Use a natural shade; expect a tint, not full cover; follow the maker.

ul: Semi-permanent colour is often a **good choice**: no ammonia in most types and no lightening, so it is gentle on dry, fragile coils.
Detangle gently first, from the ends up, with a wide-tooth comb or fingers. Keep tension low.
Tight coils hide hair. Work in **small sections** and check the colour has reached every hair, including the underside of each section and the nape.
Do not pile coily hair on top of the head and rub the colour in; press and smooth it through each section.
Check the edges and hairline for thinning and traction damage before you put colour near them.
Relaxed lengths are usually more porous than the new growth. Do a strand test on both.
Follow the maker's rule on how long to wait between a relaxer and a colour service. Colour on a relaxer that is only a day or two old, or on a scalp that is irritated, is not safe.
Look for the line of demarcation: colour may take differently on either side of it.

blocks.note: After colour, the hair needs moisture. Plan a conditioning treatment, and tell the client that a colour-safe moisturising conditioner will help the colour last and the hair stay soft.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Item
Use
rows: Shade chart or swatch book
Choosing the shade and the level.
Plastic or glass bowl; applicator bottle; tint brush
Mixing (if needed) and applying. Never metal bowls; metal can react with some products.
Tail comb; sectioning clips
Parting the hair into neat sections.
Gloves; apron; towels; colour cape; neck strips
Protection for you and the client; a fresh towel for each client.
Barrier cream
A film on the skin at the hairline and ears that prevents staining.
Timer
Timing the processing exactly. Do not guess.
Cotton wool; skin stain remover; damp cloth
Taking colour off the skin.
Plastic cap; heat source (only if the maker says)
Help the colour enter the hair evenly.

flow: Wash your hands; check the skin test and scalp
Put on gloves and an apron
Gown the client with a towel and a colour cape
Put barrier cream along the hairline, on the ears and the back of the neck
Shampoo with a gentle shampoo and towel-dry, unless the maker says otherwise
Comb through gently and section the hair into four

ul: **Shampoo first, no heavy conditioner.** Clean hair takes colour evenly. A heavy conditioner can coat the hair and block the colour.
Most semi-permanent colours go on **damp, towel-dried hair**. Some makers say dry hair; follow the maker.
Take care with the hairline and edges: they are fine, take colour fast and are easily stained.

flow: Check the colour is mixed and ready as the maker says
Take a small sub-section with the tail comb
Apply the colour with the brush or applicator bottle from roots to ends, evenly
Work it gently through with your gloved fingers
Move to the next sub-section; keep a steady order
Check the underside and the nape for missed hair
Start the timer when the last section is covered, or when the maker says

ul: Work in an even order so you do not miss patches and the first part does not process longer than the last.
Use enough colour to cover every strand, and no more. Colour that drips is wasted and stains.
If the hair is porous at the ends, you may apply to the roots first and the ends last, as the maker allows.
Never mix products from different makers.
Process for **exactly the time the maker says**. Set a timer and check the client often.
Too short a time gives a weak colour; too long usually gives a darker result on porous hair and does not make the colour last longer.
Use a plastic cap or gentle heat **only if the maker says**. They help the colour enter evenly; too much heat can irritate the scalp or dry the hair.
Stay with the client. If her scalp itches, burns or tingles painfully, rinse the colour off at once and tell the instructor.

flow: Check a strand: wipe off a little colour and look at the shade
Rinse with lukewarm or cool water until the water runs clear
Do not shampoo hard unless the maker says to
Condition with a colour-safe, moisturising conditioner if the maker allows
Remove skin stains with the stain remover
Dry and style gently, then check the colour is even from roots to ends

blocks.note: The maker may tell you to apply a colour-sealing conditioner or an acid rinse at the end. Follow the maker. Never shampoo hard straight after rinsing: it can wash out some of the new colour.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Protection
Why
rows: Gloves (nitrile or vinyl, as the Centre says)
Protect your skin from stains and allergy. Colour can cause dermatitis with repeated contact.
Apron
Protects your clothes.
Colour cape and towel
Protect the client's clothes and neck.
Barrier cream at the hairline and ears
Stops stains and keeps colour off the skin.
Good ventilation
Clears fumes so nobody breathes them in.
Neck strip or cotton wool
Keeps the cape from touching colour and the skin.

ul: Read the label and the maker's instructions every time. Read the safety data sheet for hazardous products.
Never mix brands or products the maker does not allow, and never use a product from an unlabelled bottle.
Wipe up spills at once, so nobody slips. Colour on the floor also stains.
Keep colour away from the eyes, and from broken skin.
Do not eat, drink or smoke in the colour area. Wash your hands after removing gloves.
Keep products and mixed colour away from children, food and heat.

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Colour on the skin (not the eyes)
Wipe it off at once with damp cotton wool or a damp cloth; use a skin stain remover if it has stained.
Colour in the eye

Rinse the eye immediately with plenty of clean, cool running water for at least 10 to 15 minutes, with the lid held open and the water running away from the other eye. Get medical help and tell the instructor. Do not rub.
Itching, burning or redness of the scalp during or after the service
Rinse the colour off at once with cool water, tell the instructor, and record it. Do not use that product again on her.
A rash, swelling or difficulty breathing
Stop, rinse, call the instructor and first aider; if breathing is affected, call for emergency help (the ambulance in Jamaica is 110) at once.
Colour spilled on a client's clothes
Blot (do not rub), tell her, and follow the salon's policy on damage.

ul: Store opened products **capped tightly, labelled, in a cool, dark place** away from heat and sunlight.
Use the oldest stock first; check dates.
Mix only what you need, in a clean plastic bowl or bottle. Never pour leftover colour back into the bottle.
Throw away leftover mixed colour as the maker and the Centre's rules say. Do not flush large amounts down a drain without checking the rule.
Used gloves, neck strips and cotton wool go in the bin; sharp items in a sharps box.

head: Word
What it means
rows: Cleaning
Removing dirt, hair and product with soap and water. It always comes first.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical to kill most germs on a clean tool or surface, for the full contact time on the label.
Sterilising
Killing all germs including spores, with special equipment such as an autoclave.

ul: Wash bowls, brushes, combs and clips in warm, soapy water to remove all colour and hair. Rinse, then put them in disinfectant for the contact time. Dry and store in a clean, covered place.
Fresh towel and cape for every client; used ones go straight into a closed laundry bin.
Wipe the trolley, chair and basin with disinfectant.

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat and humidity are hard on colour products. Never leave bottles in a sunny window, in a hot car or beside a dryer.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Advice
Why
rows: Use a gentle, colour-safe shampoo and conditioner
Strong shampoos strip colour.
Wash with lukewarm or cool water; do not wash more often than needed
Hot water opens the cuticle and lets colour out.
Protect from sun, sea water and chlorine: hat, scarf, rinse after swimming
Sun and salt dry the hair and fade colour; chlorine can change the tone.
Use a heat protectant and low heat
Heat dulls and fades colour.
Moisture: a weekly deep conditioning treatment for dry or natural hair
Keeps hair soft and the colour shiny.
Sleep on a satin scarf, bonnet or pillowcase
Cotton rubs and dries the hair.
Book a refresh in a few weeks
The colour fades gradually; a refresh keeps it even.

blocks.p: Be honest about fading. Say, 'It will fade over a number of shampoos, as the maker says,' rather than giving a number of weeks as a promise. Faster fading is normal on porous hair and with hot water and sun.

ul: Date; client; stylist.
Skin test: date, product, result.
Strand test: result.
Natural level, tone and grey; porosity; history.
Shade and maker; whether any developer or activator was used; the amount.
Processing time; whether a cap or heat was used.
The result and the client's comments.
Aftercare and products advised; the client's agreement.

blocks.p: Records mean the next stylist can repeat or adjust the colour exactly, and they show that tests were done. Keep them confidential.

flow: With gloves still on, throw away leftover mixed colour as the maker says
Cap and wipe the bottles; put them in a cool, dark store, labels out
Wash, rinse, disinfect, dry and store the bowls, brushes, combs and clips
Put the towels and cape in the laundry; bin neck strips and cotton wool
Wipe the basin, chair and trolley; sweep hair and mop spills
Remove gloves, wash your hands, and finish the record card

blocks.note: Check the finished colour in daylight if you can. Look for even colour from roots to ends, no missed patches, no stains on the skin, and a shade that matches what you agreed. If it is wrong, tell the instructor before the client leaves.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: I can say how semi-permanent colour differs from temporary and permanent colour, and what it can and cannot do.
I can explain why it fades gradually and leaves no regrowth line.
I can find the natural level and tone and use the level system and a shade chart.
I can use the colour wheel to cancel a brassy or orange tone.
I can choose a shade at the client's level or darker, and tell her honestly what she will see.
I can carry out a consultation and recognise contra-indications that mean postponing the service.
I can do and read a skin test and a strand test, and say when they are needed.
I can explain how porosity changes the colour result and what to do about it.
I can adapt the service for natural, coily and relaxed hair.
I can gown and protect the client, wear PPE, and put barrier cream on correctly.
I can shampoo, section, apply colour evenly, time it and rinse until clear.
I can explain why a heavy conditioner or hard shampooing spoils the result.
I can handle colour on skin, in the eyes, and a scalp reaction.
I can store, handle and throw away colour products safely, and clean, disinfect and store tools.
I can give aftercare advice, suggest suitable products and fill in the record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the step and the reason: 'I do a strand test on the ends because they are porous and may take the colour darker.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A colour that deposits tone on and just under the cuticle; it cannot lighten and fades over a number of shampoos.
Adds colour without lightening the hair.
A rinse, spray or mousse that coats the outside of the hair and washes out at the next shampoo.
An oxidative colour mixed with developer; it can lighten and lasts until the hair is cut or grows out.
How light or dark hair is, on a scale from 1 (black) to 10 (lightest blonde).
The colour you see in the hair: warm, cool or neutral.
Opposites on the colour wheel, which cancel each other.
How easily the hair takes in and loses water and products.
A small amount of colour on the skin, left for the maker's time, to check for allergy.
Colour put on a small section to see the final shade and timing.
A cream on the skin at the hairline and ears that prevents staining.
Personal protective equipment: gloves, apron and any other protection.
The time a disinfectant must stay wet on a tool to work.
The maker's sheet on a product's hazards, storage and first aid.

c1.title: A first colour for a student in Mandeville
c1.text: Kimberly Chambers, 17, a sixth-form student in Mandeville, wants her very dark natural hair (level 2) to look 'bright cherry red' for her graduation in three weeks. She has never coloured her hair. Her hair is natural, coily and healthy, though dry at the ends. She says she is allergic to a hair gel she used last year and 'came out in a rash'. Trainee Shanel has the maker's chart, and the maker's leaflet says to do a skin test 48 hours before the service.

c2.title: Uneven ends in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Mrs. Beverley Walters, 44, comes to a salon in Ocho Rios for a refresh of her dark brown semi-permanent colour. Her hair is relaxed, shoulder-length and her last relaxer was five weeks ago. The roots and the first 10 cm are smooth, but the last 8 cm of the ends feel rough and dry and soak up water fast. Last time, she says, the ends came out 'much darker than the top' and she was not happy. Trainee Dwayne wants to avoid a repeat.

c3.title: Brassy colour in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: Alicia Morgan, 31, wears her natural hair in a short cut. Her hair is level 3 with an orange-brown, brassy tone, left from a permanent colour done by a friend months ago. She wants it to look a 'cooler, darker brown'. Her scalp is healthy and the skin test is clear. Trainee Peter selects a level 3 ash brown semi-permanent colour. He does not use a timer and plans to check by looking at the colour from time to time.

c4.title: A busy colour station in Montego Bay
c4.text: At a salon in Montego Bay, trainee Kemar has finished a semi-permanent colour on Mrs. Hopeton. As he rinses her, she says that her scalp is itching and feels hot, and her forehead looks red. Earlier, Kemar had put barrier cream on the hairline but did not wear gloves. At the colour station, a half-used bottle of colour has been left uncapped on the sunny windowsill, and a bowl of mixed colour has been poured back into the bottle.

c5.title: Grey and aftercare in Black River
c5.text: Mr. Norman Dixon, 58, a retired teacher in Black River, has grey patches at his temples and wants a natural look with no hard line. He swims at the sea nearly every day and washes his hair daily with a strong shampoo and hot water. He asks Danielle, the trainee, how long a semi-permanent colour will last and how to look after it.

questions.q: What should Shanel tell Kimberly about the bright cherry red on her level 2 hair?
o: It will look bright if left on for double the time the maker says
It will look bright if it is mixed with a stronger developer
It will show as a slight red tint in strong light, because the colour cannot lighten
It will look the same as on the chart, because the chart shows the colour on every hair
questions.why: Semi-permanent colour deposits only, so on very dark hair a bright red shows as a tint. Longer time and a stronger developer do not make it lighten, and the chart shows the shade on hair of a stated level.

questions.q: Kimberly's past rash from a hair gel means what for Shanel's testing?
o: A skin test as the maker says; a reaction rules out the product
A strand test is enough, because the rash came from a gel, not a colour
No test is needed, since a gel and a colour are different kinds of product
A skin test, but only if her scalp feels itchy on the day
questions.why: A past reaction to a hair product is a warning. Semi-permanent colour can still cause allergy, so the skin test the maker requires must be done, and a reaction means no colour with that product.

questions.q: How far ahead of the service should Shanel do the skin test in this case?
o: On the day of the service, a few minutes before
A week before, so that any reaction can fade
About one hour before, while the hair is being shampooed
About 48 hours before, as the maker's leaflet says
questions.why: Makers' leaflets give the test time, often 48 hours, because an allergic reaction can take a day or two to show. Always follow the leaflet in front of you.

questions.q: Kimberly's skin test is clear. Which is the best advice for the shade, if she still wants a visible change?
o: Choose a lighter shade and leave it on longer so it shows
Explain that a different service to lighten the hair would come first
Choose the bright red shade anyway and tell her it will fade soon
Put it on just before her next relaxer, since relaxing helps colour take
questions.why: Showing a bright shade on level 2 hair needs the hair to be lightened first, which is a different service. Being honest early prevents disappointment and damage. Choosing a lighter shade or a longer time cannot change the result.

questions.q: Why did the ends turn out darker than the roots last time?
o: The ends were relaxed more recently than the roots
The ends are porous and soak up more colour
The ends were washed with hotter water
The developer was stronger on the ends
questions.why: Hair that feels rough and soaks up water has a raised cuticle, so it takes in more colour and turns out darker. Semi-permanent colour generally uses no developer.

questions.q: What should Dwayne do before colouring Mrs. Walters's hair?
o: Apply the colour to the whole head at once and rinse the ends earlier
Apply a heavy conditioner to the ends to fill them in, then colour all over
Choose a darker shade for the roots so that the roots and ends look matched
Strand test the porous ends, then adjust order or time as the maker allows
questions.why: A strand test on the most porous part shows how dark it will go. You can then colour the roots first, give the ends less time, or pre-treat as the maker allows. A heavy conditioner can block the colour unpredictably.

questions.q: Mrs. Walters's relaxer was five weeks ago. What is the correct approach to the gap between the relaxer and the colour?
o: Follow the maker's rule on the gap after a relaxer; check the scalp
Ignore the gap, since semi-permanent colour is gentle on any scalp
Colour straight away, as relaxed hair takes colour best on the same day
Wait six full months before any kind of colour goes on relaxed hair
questions.why: Makers give the gap and it varies. Five weeks is likely to be outside any 'too soon' period, but you still check the maker's rule and the scalp. Same-day colour on a relaxed scalp risks irritation.

questions.q: Why does Peter's choice of an ash brown suit Alicia's orange-brown hair?
o: Ash tones are warm and add more orange
Ash tones are neutral and have no effect on tone
Ash tones are cool, and blue cancels orange
Ash tones are red and cover brassy colour
questions.why: Ash colours contain blue or green, the opposite of orange and red on the colour wheel, so they neutralise brassiness and give a cooler brown.

questions.q: What is wrong with Peter's plan to check the time by eye?
o: Nothing wrong, because semi-permanent colour cannot over-process
He should leave it on for as long as it takes to look dark enough
He should time it by the first section only
Processing is timed exactly as the maker says, with a timer
questions.why: Time is part of the maker's formula. Too short gives weak colour, too long can darken porous hair, and a timer is the only reliable way to keep to the maker's time.

questions.q: Alicia's hair is level 3 and Peter has chosen a level 3 shade. Why is this level a sensible choice?
o: It can lighten, but by one level only
It can only match her level or go darker
Level 3 shades contain developer and so can lighten
Level 3 is the only level that works on natural hair
questions.why: Because the colour cannot lighten, the shade must be at the hair's own level or darker, or it will not show. Level 3 matches her natural level.

questions.q: What should Kemar do first when Mrs. Hopeton complains of itching and heat?
o: Carry on with the service, because the colour is nearly finished anyway
Put more barrier cream on her forehead and hairline and carry on
Rinse the colour off at once, then tell the instructor straight away
Finish the rinse quickly and see whether the itching settles
questions.why: Itching, heat or redness during or after colour is a possible reaction. Rinse at once, tell the instructor, and record it so that product is not used again on her.

questions.q: What was wrong with Kemar's protection of himself and the client?
o: He worked without gloves, which protect against stains
He put barrier cream on the hairline, which should never be done
He rinsed the hair before the processing time was fully up
He mixed the colour in a plastic bowl instead of a metal one
questions.why: Gloves protect the stylist's skin from stains, dermatitis and allergy. Barrier cream is correct for the client's hairline, and plastic is the right bowl material.

questions.q: What is the correct way to deal with the half-used bottle left on the windowsill and the poured-back bowl of colour?
o: Store it capped, cool and dark; bin the mixed colour as the maker says
Cap the bottle where it is, and top it up with the colour left in the bowl
Leave the bottle on the sill and pour the bowl's colour away tomorrow
Put both out in the sun to dry out, then bin the empty containers
questions.why: Heat and light spoil colour, and mixed colour must never be poured back because it is contaminated and has begun to work. Store capped, labelled, cool and dark, and dispose of leftovers as the maker says.

questions.q: Which action fits the safe way to handle the colour that splashed on Mrs. Hopeton's cheek?
o: Leave it to fade, as the colour is only semi-permanent
Scrub it hard with a nail brush until the stain lifts
Wipe it off at once with damp cotton wool or a cloth
Wash her face with the same shampoo used on her hair
questions.why: Colour on the skin (not the eyes) is wiped off straight away with damp cotton wool, and a skin stain remover can be used for any stain. Scrubbing irritates the skin.

questions.q: How long should Danielle say Mr. Dixon's colour will last?
o: Exactly six weeks, in the same way as a permanent colour
It fades over a number of shampoos, as the maker says
For ever, or until the hair is cut off at the ends
Until the next shampoo, as with a temporary colour rinse
questions.why: Semi-permanent colour fades gradually and the rate varies. Honest advice is that it fades over a number of washes and fades faster with sun, salt, hot water and strong shampoo.

questions.q: Which aftercare change would help most, given his daily sea swimming and hot washes?
o: Wash twice a day with a strong clarifying shampoo to remove the salt
Wear a swimming cap only if the colour has been on for a week
Use more heat styling each week to seal the colour into the hair
Rinse after swimming; use colour-safe shampoo and lukewarm water
questions.why: Salt, sun, hot water and strong shampoo all fade colour. Rinsing after swimming, using a gentle colour-safe shampoo and cooler water protect the colour.

questions.q: What can Danielle honestly tell Mr. Dixon about the grey at his temples?
o: It will be covered completely, so that no grey shows at all afterwards
It will be softened and blended, but grey may take less colour
It will go black within a few days, however light his hair is
It will not take any colour, because grey hair is dead hair
questions.why: Semi-permanent colour tints grey and blends it, without a regrowth line, but resistant grey may be only partly covered or fade faster. It does not cover all grey.

questions.q: A trainee wants to apply a heavy conditioner to the client's hair just before the colour, 'to protect it'. What is the best response?
o: Explain that heavy conditioner can coat the hair and block the colour
Agree, because a conditioner always protects the hair before any colour
Suggest a light oil instead, because oil never blocks colour from entering
Suggest leaving the conditioner in while the colour processes on top
questions.why: Clean hair takes colour evenly. A heavy conditioner can coat the cuticle and stop colour entering, which can make the result patchy.

questions.q: Which statement about the colour wheel is correct?
o: Red and violet are opposites and cancel each other
Yellow and orange are opposites and cancel each other
Blue and violet are opposites and cancel each other
Red and green are opposites and cancel each other
questions.why: Red and green sit opposite on the wheel, as do blue with orange and yellow with violet. Opposites cancel each other, which is how an unwanted tone is neutralised.

questions.q: A client has a sore, weeping area on her scalp on the day of her colour appointment. What should the trainee do?
o: Colour the rest of the head but keep the colour off the sore area
Put the colour on as normal and rinse it off after half the time
Postpone the service, and suggest a doctor if it stays sore
Cover the sore with barrier cream and then colour as normal
questions.why: Colour on broken or weeping skin can sting, burn or let infection in. A sore, weeping area is a reason to postpone and, if it persists, to suggest a doctor.
